title: Why Am I Always Thirsty? Excessive Thirst Causes, Urgent Signs and the Tests That Check Them
summary: Always thirsty? See which signs of excessive thirst need urgent care, everyday causes, and how glucose, calcium, sodium and kidney tests find the cause.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Being thirsty all the time usually has an everyday cause: hot weather, exercise and sweating, a salty meal, or fluid lost to vomiting, diarrhea or a fever** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \]. Thirst is the body’s signal to replace lost water, so drinking until the thirst goes away is usually the right response \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \].


**When excessive thirst is ongoing and has no clear explanation, the main medical causes are high blood sugar from diabetes, diabetes insipidus, a high blood calcium level, a low blood potassium level, some medicines and, less often, kidney disease** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Doctors call this excessive thirst polydipsia. Blood and urine tests separate these causes: glucose and HbA1c for blood sugar, sodium and osmolality for water balance, calcium and potassium for the electrolyte causes, and creatinine, eGFR and a urinalysis for the kidneys \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].


## When excessive thirst needs urgent care


**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if extreme thirst comes with confusion or drowsiness, fruity-smelling breath, nausea and vomiting, deep or fast breathing, or trouble breathing** \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000304.htm) \]. In someone with diabetes, or someone who may have it without knowing, these can be signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000304.htm) \]. Both are medical emergencies \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000304.htm) \]. DKA is sometimes the first sign of type 1 diabetes \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \].


**Call 911 for severe dehydration: fainting or loss of consciousness, new confusion or a seizure, a fever over 102°F (38.8°C), or signs of heatstroke such as a rapid pulse or fast breathing** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \]. Other signs of severe dehydration include passing no urine or very dark urine, dizziness, and a rapid heartbeat \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \].


**Contact a provider soon if** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]:


- your excessive thirst is ongoing and unexplained;
- the thirst comes with blurred vision, unusual tiredness or weight loss you did not try for;
- you are passing more than 5 quarts (4.75 liters) of urine a day;
- you have diabetes and your thirst or urination has lasted a day or more.


A blood test you order yourself is not the right next step for any of the emergency signs above. They need to be assessed in person right away.


## Everyday causes of being thirsty all the time


**Most thirst follows fluid loss or a recent meal, and settles once you drink** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \]. The common everyday causes are:


- **Heat and exercise.** Sweating a lot, for example when exercising in hot weather, is one of the main ways the body loses fluid \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \]. Signs of mild to moderate dehydration include thirst, a dry or sticky mouth, passing little urine, darker yellow urine, headache and muscle cramps \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \].
- **Salt.** A recent salty or spicy meal is a listed cause of excessive thirst \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \].
- **Illness.** Fever, vomiting and diarrhea all drain body fluid \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \].
- **Caffeine and alcohol.** Caffeine is a common cause of needing to urinate more often, and alcohol is a less common one \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. The extra fluid lost has to be replaced.
- **Pregnancy.** Gestational diabetes usually causes no symptoms and is found on routine prenatal screening, but mild symptoms such as increased thirst can occur \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000896.htm) \]. A rare type of diabetes insipidus can also start in pregnancy \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \].


**Thirst with a clear trigger that goes away once you drink does not need a blood test.** The tests below are for thirst that keeps returning without an explanation \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \].


## Dry mouth or true thirst?


**A dry mouth and true thirst feel similar but are different problems.** Dry mouth, called xerostomia, means you are not making enough saliva to keep your mouth wet \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/drymouth.html) \]. True thirst is the body’s urge to replace water it has lost \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. Everyone has a dry mouth now and then, for example when nervous or stressed, but a mouth that is dry all or most of the time is a separate problem \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/drymouth.html) \].


The difference matters because a dry mouth often comes from medicines, while true thirst more often points to fluid loss or a change in blood chemistry. Diabetes can cause both \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/drymouth.html) \]\[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \].


**Medicines as a class are a common cause of both.** Hundreds of medicines can reduce saliva, including some for high blood pressure, depression and bladder control \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/drymouth.html) \]. Medicines listed as causes of excessive thirst include anticholinergics, diuretics (water pills), phenothiazines and demeclocycline \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. Lithium, used for bipolar disorder, can stop the kidneys from responding to the hormone that holds on to water, a form of diabetes insipidus \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Thiazide diuretics and lithium can also raise blood calcium \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \], and diuretics are a common cause of low potassium \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]. Talk with your prescriber before changing any medicine you think is behind your thirst.


## Excessive thirst and diabetes: glucose and HbA1c


**Feeling very thirsty is one of the common symptoms of diabetes, along with urinating more, blurred vision and fatigue** \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]. When blood sugar is too high, the kidneys try to remove the extra glucose by passing it in the urine \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. That pulls water out with it, and the lost water drives thirst \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000304.htm) \].


Type 1 diabetes symptoms usually develop quickly, over a few days or weeks, and can include weight loss without trying \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]. Type 2 diabetes symptoms can develop slowly, over several years, and many people have none \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]. Very high blood sugar that goes untreated can lead to the emergencies described above \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000320.htm) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000304.htm) \].


**Three blood tests check for diabetes** \[[13](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/tests-diagnosis) \]:


- **[Fasting plasma glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/glucose) .** Measured after at least 8 hours without food. 99 mg/dL or below is normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL is prediabetes, and 126 mg/dL or above is diabetes.
- **[HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hba1c) .** Your average blood glucose over the last 3 months, so no fasting is needed. Below 5.7% is normal, 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes, and 6.5% or above is diabetes. HbA1c may be unreliable in the second or third trimester of pregnancy and with some types of anemia or hemoglobin variants.
- **Random plasma glucose.** Used when someone has symptoms. 200 mg/dL or above suggests diabetes.


A doctor usually uses a second test to confirm diabetes \[[13](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/tests-diagnosis) \]. A urinalysis adds a quick clue: glucose is normally not detectable in urine, so[glucose in the urine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-glucose) suggests blood sugar is high enough that the kidneys are passing the extra glucose into the urine \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. For more, see[symptoms of high glucose](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-glucose) ,[the two key blood tests for diabetes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/testing-for-diabetes-the-two-key-blood-tests-you-should-know) and[why HbA1c is such a useful marker](https://mitohealth.com/blog/hba1c-best-biomarker-diabetes-working-adults) . Mito offers a[glucose blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/glucose) and an[HbA1c blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/hemoglobin-a1c-with-reflex-to-1-5-anhydroglucitol-1-5-ag) .


## Diabetes insipidus: sodium, osmolality and urine concentration


**Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a rare condition in which the body makes too much dilute urine, and people with it often feel thirsty all the time** \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Most people make 1 to 3 quarts of urine a day, and people with DI can make up to 20 quarts \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. The thirst can be intense, often with a craving for ice water, and the urine is very pale \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].


**Diabetes insipidus is not diabetes mellitus.** Both cause thirst and more urine, but in DI blood glucose is normal \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. The problem is a hormone called vasopressin, or antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which tells the kidneys to hold on to water \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]. In central DI the body does not make enough of it. In nephrogenic DI the kidneys do not respond to it, which can be caused by lithium, a high calcium level, a low potassium level or, rarely, chronic kidney disease \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Because the shared word “diabetes” causes confusion, endocrine societies proposed in 2022 renaming central DI arginine vasopressin deficiency and nephrogenic DI arginine vasopressin resistance \[[15](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470458/) \].


**DI is checked with blood and urine tests that measure water balance** \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]:


- **[Sodium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/sodium) .** A high blood sodium level can be a sign of dehydration, kidney disease or, less commonly, DI \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/sodium-blood-test/) \]. See[symptoms of high sodium](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-sodium) .
- **[Serum osmolality](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/serum-osmolality) .** This measures how concentrated the blood is, and is ordered for excessive thirst and excessive urination. Normal values are about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg, though ranges vary by lab. A high result can mean DI, high blood sugar, high sodium or dehydration. A low result can mean drinking too much water or a low sodium level \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \]. Mito offers an[osmolality blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/osmolality) .
- **Urine concentration.** Urine osmolality and[urine specific gravity](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-specific-gravity) show how concentrated the urine is. A low result can mean DI, drinking too much fluid or kidney failure \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003609.htm) \]\[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003587.htm) \]. Specific gravity is usually part of a routine urinalysis \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003587.htm) \].


**These tests can raise the question of DI but do not confirm it.** Confirming DI and its type takes specialized testing done under medical supervision, usually with an endocrinologist or nephrologist \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \].


## High calcium and low potassium


**A high blood calcium level (hypercalcemia) can cause increased thirst and more frequent urination, because it changes how the kidneys work** \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. Most people with high calcium have no symptoms, and it is most often found on routine blood tests \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. When symptoms happen, they can include nausea, constipation, muscle weakness, tiredness or confusion, and bone pain \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \].


The most common cause is an overactive parathyroid gland, and high calcium is most common in women over 50 \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. Other causes include too much vitamin D, thiazide diuretics, lithium, some cancers and being low on fluids \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. A[calcium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/calcium) result that is high is followed by tests such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. See[symptoms of high calcium](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-calcium) ,[hyperparathyroidism symptoms and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/hyperparathyroidism-symptoms-and-blood-tests) and[whether high calcium is a sign of cancer](https://mitohealth.com/blog/is-high-calcium-a-sign-of-cancer) . Mito offers a standalone[calcium blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/calcium) .


**A low blood potassium level (hypokalemia) that persists can stop the kidneys from concentrating urine, so you pass more urine and become thirsty as a result** \[[20](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/endocrine-and-metabolic-disorders/electrolyte-disorders/hypokalemia) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Common causes include diuretics, vomiting or diarrhea, laxative overuse, heavy sweating and some hormone conditions \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]. A small drop often causes no symptoms. Larger drops can cause muscle weakness or cramps, tiredness, constipation and a feeling of skipped heartbeats \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]. The normal blood[potassium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/potassium) range is about 3.5 to 5.1 mEq/L \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]. Contact a provider right away if you take a diuretic and have these symptoms, or if you have had heavy vomiting or diarrhea \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]. See[symptoms of low potassium](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-potassium) and[electrolyte imbalance symptoms](https://mitohealth.com/guide/electrolyte-imbalance-symptoms) .


## Thirst and kidney disease: creatinine, eGFR and urinalysis


**Kidney disease is a less common cause of excessive thirst.** Kidney failure is a listed cause, and chronic kidney disease can rarely cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Most people with early chronic kidney disease (CKD) have no symptoms, and the only way to know is with blood and urine tests \[[21](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \]. In advanced CKD, how often you urinate can change \[[21](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \].


The tests that check the kidneys are:


- **[Creatinine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/creatinine) and[eGFR](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/egfrcr) .** Creatinine is a waste product from muscle that the kidneys remove from the blood, and its level is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). A GFR of 60 or more is in the normal range, less than 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less is kidney failure \[[22](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \].
- **Urinalysis.** A urinalysis checks urine concentration (specific gravity), glucose, ketones and protein in one sample \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]. Dilute urine with a low specific gravity can come from kidney failure as well as from DI or drinking a lot of fluid \[[19](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003587.htm) \].


For the other signs that point to the kidneys, see[kidney disease symptoms and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/kidney-disease-symptoms-and-blood-tests) .


## Habitual drinking, and feeling thirstier after drinking water


**Drinking far more water than the body needs, as a habit, is its own cause of a constant urge to drink.** Doctors call it primary polydipsia \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]. One type, sometimes called compulsive water drinking, is seen mostly in people who consciously drink large amounts of water to stay healthy, and it has become more common with the popularity of lifestyle programs \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]. Another type is linked to some mental health conditions \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]. The main condition doctors need to tell it apart from is diabetes insipidus \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \].


The risk with heavy habitual drinking is a low blood sodium level (hyponatremia), which is a serious complication \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]. A low serum osmolality and a low sodium both fit drinking too much water \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \].


**Feeling thirsty again soon after a glass of water is not a diagnosis on its own, but three patterns fit it:**


- **Water is passing straight through.** In diabetes and in DI, fluid leaves in the urine, so thirst returns quickly \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. Thirst that does not settle with drinking and keeps coming back is the “ongoing and unexplained” thirst worth checking \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \].
- **The mouth is dry, not the body.** A dry mouth comes from too little saliva, which is a different problem from losing body water \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/drymouth.html) \]\[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. In one type of DI driven by the thirst center, sucking on ice chips or sugar-free candies to moisten the mouth may help reduce thirst \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \].
- **The habit itself.** Drinking a lot can become routine, and the large volume of dilute urine it causes is the same pattern doctors look for in primary polydipsia \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \].


## Which tests check the cause of excessive thirst


**MedlinePlus lists the tests a provider may order for excessive thirst: blood glucose, serum calcium, serum sodium, serum osmolality, a complete blood count, a urinalysis and urine osmolality** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. Each likely cause maps to specific results:


Likely cause What points to it Tests that check it


Heat, exercise, salt or illness A clear trigger, dark urine, settles after drinking \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000982.htm) \] None if it settles


High blood sugar or diabetes Thirst with more urine, blurred vision, fatigue, weight loss \[[7](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \] Fasting glucose, HbA1c, urine glucose \[[13](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/tests-diagnosis) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]


Diabetes insipidus Large volumes of very pale urine, craving for cold water \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \] Sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality or specific gravity \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]


High calcium Often none; sometimes constipation, weakness, tiredness \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \] Calcium, then PTH and vitamin D \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]


Low potassium Diuretic use, vomiting or diarrhea, muscle weakness or cramps \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \] Potassium \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \]


Kidney disease Often none until advanced \[[21](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \] Creatinine and eGFR, urinalysis \[[22](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]


Habitual heavy drinking Drinking large amounts by habit, dilute urine \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \] Sodium, serum osmolality \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]\[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \]


### What each result pattern suggests


- **High fasting glucose or HbA1c, with glucose in the urine,** points to diabetes \[[13](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/tests-diagnosis) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \].
- **Normal glucose with a high serum osmolality or sodium and very dilute urine** fits diabetes insipidus, which then needs specialist confirmation \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \]\[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003609.htm) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].
- **Low sodium, low serum osmolality and dilute urine** fits drinking too much water, as in primary polydipsia \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \]\[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \].
- **High calcium** points to the parathyroid glands, vitamin D or another calcium cause \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \].
- **Low potassium** points to potassium loss, often from a diuretic or the gut \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000479.htm) \].
- **A low eGFR with a high creatinine** points to the kidneys \[[22](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \].
- **High sodium with concentrated urine** fits plain dehydration \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/sodium-blood-test/) \]\[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003609.htm) \].
- **All normal** makes the medical causes above less likely, which leaves everyday causes, medicines and dry mouth. A provider can sort these out with your history.


### Mito tests for excessive thirst


- The **[Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)](https://mitohealth.com/products/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp)** covers several thirst causes in one blood draw: glucose for blood sugar, sodium and potassium, calcium, and creatinine and urea nitrogen (BUN) for the kidneys, plus chloride, carbon dioxide, albumin, total protein and liver tests. The CMP measures 14 substances in one blood sample \[[24](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp/) \], and creatinine is the basis for the eGFR estimate \[[22](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/tests-diagnosis) \]. It does not measure osmolality, HbA1c or urine concentration.
- The **[Basic Metabolic Panel (BMP)](https://mitohealth.com/products/basic-metabolic-panel-bmp)** is a smaller panel of 8 markers: glucose, sodium, potassium, chloride, carbon dioxide, calcium, BUN and creatinine, without the liver tests.
- The **[HbA1c blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/hemoglobin-a1c-with-reflex-to-1-5-anhydroglucitol-1-5-ag)** adds your 3-month average blood sugar to a single glucose reading.
- The **[osmolality blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/osmolality)** measures serum osmolality, a water-balance marker the CMP does not include.
- The **[complete urinalysis](https://mitohealth.com/products/urinalysis-complete-with-reflex-to-culture)** checks urine glucose, specific gravity, ketones and protein.


## When thirst and urine output rise together


**Thirst and passing a lot of urine often travel together, and the order matters.** In diabetes and diabetes insipidus, the body loses water in the urine first, and thirst follows to replace it \[[3](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/diabetes-insipidus) \]. In primary polydipsia, the drinking comes first, and the extra urine follows \[[23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562251/) \]. The blood tests above help tell these apart: a high sodium and osmolality fits water loss, and a low sodium and osmolality fits too much water in \[[17](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003463.htm) \]\[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/sodium-blood-test/) \].


If needing to pee often is your main symptom, with or without thirst, see[frequent urination: why am I peeing so much?](https://mitohealth.com/blog/frequent-urination) , which covers urinary infections, overactive bladder and an enlarged prostate.

## Frequently asked questions


### What does diabetic thirst feel like?


There is no special kind of thirst that only diabetes causes. With high blood sugar, people usually feel very thirsty and also urinate more, and may have blurred vision, fatigue or, in type 1 diabetes, weight loss without trying. Type 1 symptoms often appear over days or weeks, while type 2 symptoms can build slowly over years or be absent. A fasting glucose or HbA1c blood test is how diabetes is checked.


### When should I worry about excessive thirst?


Get emergency care if extreme thirst comes with confusion, drowsiness, fruity-smelling breath, nausea and vomiting, deep or fast breathing, or fainting. Contact a provider if the thirst is ongoing and unexplained, comes with blurred vision, tiredness or weight loss, or you pass more than 5 quarts (4.75 liters) of urine a day. Thirst after heat, exercise or a salty meal that settles once you drink is normal.


### What deficiency makes you thirsty?


The best-known link is a low blood potassium level, which, when it lasts, can stop the kidneys from concentrating urine, so you pass more urine and get thirsty. Too little body water itself, from sweating, vomiting, diarrhea or fever, is the most common cause of thirst. A high calcium level, the opposite of a deficiency, can also cause thirst. Potassium and calcium are both measured on a basic or comprehensive metabolic panel.


### Why am I thirstier after drinking water?


Feeling thirsty again soon after drinking usually means one of three things. With high blood sugar or diabetes insipidus, fluid passes quickly into the urine, so thirst returns. A dry mouth from too little saliva, often caused by medicines, can feel like thirst that water does not fix. Or drinking large amounts has become a habit. Thirst that keeps coming back without an explanation is worth checking with blood and urine tests.


### Can you drink too much water?


Yes. Drinking far more than the body needs, as a habit, is called primary polydipsia. It produces large amounts of dilute urine and can lower the blood sodium level, a condition called hyponatremia, which can be serious. A low sodium and a low serum osmolality on blood tests fit drinking too much water.
